Something is preposterous when it is so wildly unreasonable, so contrary to common sense, or so absurd that it almost doesn't deserve to be taken seriously. It's not just wrong — it's outrageously, almost laughably wrong or unreasonable. When something is preposterous, a typical reaction is disbelief, like: "How could anyone even suggest that?"

Think of it on a scale. "Wrong" sits at one end. Then you have "silly," then "absurd," and at the far extreme end — almost falling off the edge — you have preposterous. It describes things that are so far from logic, reason, or reality that they feel almost offensive to common sense.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Preposterous?

The word is flexible. It can describe:

Ideas or claims — "The claim that drinking bleach cures illness is preposterous." The idea is so dangerous and baseless that it's beyond mere "incorrect" — it's absurd at its core.

Demands or expectations — "It is preposterous to expect a five-year-old to run a marathon." The expectation is so wildly unreasonable that it borders on ridiculous.

Situations or behavior — "He wore a full tuxedo to the beach and insisted everyone else was dressed inappropriately. It was preposterous." The situation is so backwards and illogical that it almost seems like a joke.

Prices, rules, or conditions — "They are charging $500 for a glass of water. That is preposterous." It implies the price is so outrageously unreasonable that no sensible person could accept it.
The Emotional Flavor of the Word

This is important. Preposterous doesn't just describe something logically — it also carries an emotional charge. When someone calls something preposterous, they're often expressing:

  • Disbelief — "I can't believe anyone would even say that."
  • Indignation — "This is insulting to anyone with common sense."
  • Exasperation — "This is so ridiculous, I don't even know where to begin."

So it's not a neutral, cold, academic word. It has heat to it. When you call something preposterous, you're signaling that you find it not just incorrect, but almost outrageous in how unreasonable it is.

Very strong. This is not a word you use for small, minor unreasonableness. You wouldn't say "It's preposterous that he put too much salt in the soup." That would be an overstatement. But you would say "It's preposterous that he put salt in someone's tea and called it a drink." The degree of absurdity needs to match the strength of the word.

A good test: if something makes you genuinely stop and think "Is this real? How can anyone think this is okay?" — that's likely preposterous territory.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Absurd is the closest relative. The two are nearly interchangeable in most situations. But "preposterous" tends to feel slightly stronger and more emphatic. It has a bit more force and indignation behind it.

Ridiculous is similar too, but "ridiculous" can sometimes be used lightly or even playfully ("That hat looks ridiculous on you!"). "Preposterous" rarely goes that light — it almost always implies something more seriously unreasonable.

Ludicrous is also very close. If anything, "ludicrous" leans more into the laughable, almost comical aspect of the absurdity, while "preposterous" leans a little more into the "this defies all reason" aspect.

Outrageous focuses more on something being shocking or morally offensive. "Preposterous" focuses more specifically on something being illogical or wildly unreasonable. A lie can be outrageous (shocking); but a claim that the moon is made of cheese is preposterous (defies reason).

• It does not simply mean "unusual" or "different." Something can be unusual and perfectly reasonable. A preposterous thing is specifically unreasonable, not just rare or strange.
  • It does not just mean "wrong." A typo is wrong. A miscalculation is wrong. Preposterous implies a much grander, more glaring failure of reason or logic.
  • It does not mean "impossible" on its own. Something can be technically impossible but still be a reasonable idea based on the information available. Preposterous implies a quality of absurdity and irrationality, not just impossibility.
Register and Tone: When Do People Use This Word?

"Preposterous" is slightly formal — more at home in writing, speeches, debates, or serious conversations than in casual texting. That said, it's absolutely understood and used in everyday speech, especially when someone wants to sound emphatic and intelligent while expressing disbelief.

It's a word that has a certain weight and elegance to it. Saying "that's preposterous" in a discussion sounds more authoritative and pointed than just saying "that's stupid" or "that makes no sense." It implies that the speaker has applied reason and judgment — and finds the idea or claim to be a failure by any reasonable standard.

If you want a single sentence to anchor the meaning in your memory:

Preposterous means so absurd and contrary to reason or common sense that it's almost laughable — and anyone with a clear head would instantly recognize how unreasonable it is.

Whenever you come across an idea, demand, claim, or situation that makes you think "This is beyond ridiculous — how can anyone even say this with a straight face?" — that is your cue that the word preposterous fits perfectly.
